vtrmc-1992-01.title: Second derivative
vtrmc-1992-01.body:
By the fundamental theorem of calculus and the chain rule,
$$F'(x)=e^{(x^3)^2}\cdot3x^2=3x^2e^{x^6}.$$
Differentiating again,
$$F''(x)=6xe^{x^6}+3x^2\cdot6x^5e^{x^6}=6x\,e^{x^6}\,(1+3x^6).$$
Since $e^{x^6}(1+3x^6)>0$, the sign of $F''(x)$ is the sign of $x$: the graph is concave down for $x<0$ and concave up for $x>0$. So the only inflection point is at $x=0$, where $F(0)=\int_0^0e^{t^2}dt=0$. (Also $F'''(0)=6\ne0$.)

**Answer:** $(0,0)$.

vtrmc-1992-01.title: Symmetry
vtrmc-1992-01.body:
The integrand $e^{t^2}$ is even, so $\int_0^{-u}e^{t^2}dt=-\int_0^ue^{t^2}dt$; hence $F(-x)=-F(x)$ and $F$ is odd. For $x>0$, $F'(x)=3x^2e^{x^6}$ is a product of positive increasing functions, so $F'$ is increasing and $F$ is convex on $(0,\infty)$; by oddness $F$ is concave on $(-\infty,0)$. The concavity changes only at $0$, and $F(0)=0$.

**Answer:** $(0,0)$.

vtrmc-1992-02.title: Reflect twice
vtrmc-1992-02.body:
Let $P=(x_1,y_1)$, $Q=(x_2,y_2)$ and $Q''=(-x_2,-y_2)$, the image of $Q$ under reflection in both axes.

**Lower bound.** Take any path from $P$ to $Q$ touching the $x$-axis at $X$ and the $y$-axis at $Y$. Suppose $X$ is reached first (the other order is handled the same way, see below). A path between two points is at least as long as the segment joining them, so the length is at least $|PX|+|XY|+|YQ|$. Write $X=(s,0)$, $Y=(0,u)$.
- Reflection in the $y$-axis fixes $Y$ and sends $Q$ to $Q'=(-x_2,y_2)$, so $|YQ|=|YQ'|$, and $|XY|+|YQ'|\ge|XQ'|$.
- Reflection in the $x$-axis fixes $X$ and sends $Q'$ to $Q''$, so $|XQ'|=|XQ''|$, and $|PX|+|XQ''|\ge|PQ''|$.

Hence the length is at least $|PQ''|$. If $Y$ is reached first, reflect $Q$ first in the $x$-axis and then in the $y$-axis; the composition sends $Q$ to the same point $Q''$, and the same argument gives the same bound. So
$$l\ge|PQ''|=\sqrt{(x_1+x_2)^2+(y_1+y_2)^2}.$$

**The bound is attained.** On the segment from $P$ to $Q''$, parametrised as $P+t(Q''-P)$, $t\in[0,1]$, the $y$-coordinate vanishes at $t_x=\frac{y_1}{y_1+y_2}$ and the $x$-coordinate at $t_y=\frac{x_1}{x_1+x_2}$. The hypotheses give $x_1y_2>y_1y_2>y_1x_2$, so $t_x<t_y$: the segment first crosses the positive $x$-axis at a point $X_0$, then runs through the fourth quadrant and crosses the negative $y$-axis at $Y_0=(0,-u_0)$, $u_0>0$. Reflect the piece $X_0Y_0$ in the $x$-axis and the piece $Y_0Q''$ in both axes. We obtain the path $P\to X_0\to(0,u_0)\to Q$ made of three segments with the same total length $|PQ''|$, touching both axes. (Even without the hypotheses the minimum is the same; they just make the shortest path touch the $x$-axis first.)

**Answer:** $l=\sqrt{(x_1+x_2)^2+(y_1+y_2)^2}$.

vtrmc-1992-03.title: Use $|\sin u|\le|u|$
vtrmc-1992-03.body:
**A lemma.** $|\sin u|\le|u|$ for all real $u$, with equality only for $u=0$. Indeed $h(u)=u-\sin u$ has $h'(u)=1-\cos u\ge0$ with equality only at isolated points, so $h$ is strictly increasing; as $h(0)=0$, we get $\sin u<u$ for $u>0$, and the case $u<0$ follows because $\sin$ is odd.

**(i)** $f_2(x)=f(f(x))=1+\sin\bigl(f(x)-1\bigr)=1+\sin\bigl(\sin(x-1)\bigr)$. With $y=x-1$, the equation $f_2(x)=x$ becomes $\sin(\sin y)=y$. If this holds, then by the lemma (twice)
$$|y|=|\sin(\sin y)|\le|\sin y|\le|y|,$$
so $|\sin y|=|y|$ and $y=0$. Conversely $y=0$ is a solution. Hence $x_0=1$ is the unique point with $f_2(x_0)=x_0$.

**(ii)** $f(1)=1+\sin0=1$, so by induction $f_n(1)=1$ for all $n\ge0$. Therefore
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{f_n(x_0)}{3^n}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac1{3^n}=\frac1{1-\frac13}=\frac32.$$

**Answer:** $\frac32$.

vtrmc-1992-04.title: Monotone and bounded
vtrmc-1992-04.body:
Let $T=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$, the positive root of $x^2-x-1$, so $T^2=T+1$ and $x^2-x-1<0$ for $0\le x<T$.

**Bounds.** We show $1\le t_n<T$ by induction. It holds for $t_1=1$. If $1\le t_n<T$, then $t_{n+1}^2=1+t_n\in[2,\,1+T)=[2,T^2)$, and since $t_{n+1}>0$ this gives $\sqrt2\le t_{n+1}<T$.

**Monotonicity.** $t_{n+1}^2-t_n^2=1+t_n-t_n^2=-(t_n^2-t_n-1)>0$ because $0\le t_n<T$. As all terms are positive, $t_{n+1}>t_n$.

**Limit.** An increasing sequence bounded above converges; let $L=\lim t_n\in[1,T]$. Letting $n\to\infty$ in $t_{n+1}^2=1+t_n$ gives $L^2=1+L$, and since $L>0$, $L=T$.

**Answer:** $\lim t_n=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$.

vtrmc-1992-05.title: Diagonalise
vtrmc-1992-05.body:
The characteristic polynomial is $\det(xI-A)=x(x-3)+2=x^2-3x+2=(x-1)(x-2)$, so the eigenvalues are $1$ and $2$.

- For $1$: $(A-I)\binom uv=\begin{pmatrix}-1&-2\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\binom uv=0$ has the solution $\binom{2}{-1}$.
- For $2$: $(A-2I)\binom uv=\begin{pmatrix}-2&-2\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\binom uv=0$ has the solution $\binom{1}{-1}$.

With $T=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ we get $T^{-1}AT=\operatorname{diag}(1,2)$, and $\det T=-1$ gives $T^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\-1&-2\end{pmatrix}$. Hence
$$A^{100}=T\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&2^{100}\end{pmatrix}T^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}2&2^{100}\\-1&-2^{100}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\-1&-2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2-2^{100}&2-2^{101}\\-1+2^{100}&-1+2^{101}\end{pmatrix}.$$
(Checked by exact integer computation of $A^{100}$.)

vtrmc-1992-06.title: Factor and take a second difference
vtrmc-1992-06.body:
Since $p(r)=0$, the factor theorem gives $p(x)=(x-r)q(x)$ with $q(x)=x^2+dx+e$ a monic quadratic. For $x\ne r,\,r-1,\,r-2$ all denominators are nonzero and
$$\frac{p(x)}{x-r}=q(x),\quad\frac{p(x+1)}{x+1-r}=q(x+1),\quad\frac{p(x+2)}{x+2-r}=q(x+2).$$
So the left side equals $q(x)-2q(x+1)+q(x+2)$. Term by term:
- $x^2-2(x+1)^2+(x+2)^2=x^2-2x^2-4x-2+x^2+4x+4=2$,
- $d\bigl(x-2(x+1)+(x+2)\bigr)=0$,
- $e(1-2+1)=0$.

Hence the left side equals $2$. ∎

vtrmc-1992-07.title: Compare with an integral
vtrmc-1992-07.body:
(The base of the logarithm does not matter: changing it multiplies numerator and denominator by the same constant. Take $\log=\ln$.)

The function $x\log x$ is positive and increasing for $x>1$, so for $t\ge2$
$$\int_{t-1}^{t}x\log x\,dx\le t\log t\le\int_t^{t+1}x\log x\,dx .$$
Summing over $t=2,\dots,n$:
$$\int_1^n x\log x\,dx\le\sum_{t=2}^n t\log t\le\int_2^{n+1}x\log x\,dx.$$
With $\int x\log x\,dx=\frac{x^2\log x}{2}-\frac{x^2}{4}$:
$$\frac{n^2\log n}{2}-\frac{n^2}{4}+\frac14\le\sum_{t=2}^n t\log t\le\frac{(n+1)^2\log(n+1)}{2}-\frac{(n+1)^2}{4}-2\log2+1 .$$
Divide by $n^2\log n$. The left side tends to $\frac12$; on the right, $\frac{(n+1)^2}{n^2}\to1$ and $\frac{\log(n+1)}{\log n}\to1$, so it also tends to $\frac12$. By the squeeze theorem the limit is $\frac12$.

**Answer:** $\frac12$.

vtrmc-1992-07.title: Stolz–Cesàro
vtrmc-1992-07.body:
Let $a_n=\sum_{t=2}^nt\log t$ and $b_n=n^2\log n$, which increases to $\infty$. By the Stolz–Cesàro theorem it suffices to find the limit of
$$\frac{a_{n+1}-a_n}{b_{n+1}-b_n}=\frac{(n+1)\log(n+1)}{(n+1)^2\log(n+1)-n^2\log n}.$$
Write the denominator as $(2n+1)\log(n+1)+n^2\log\left(1+\frac1n\right)$, and note $0<n^2\log(1+\frac1n)\le n$. Dividing numerator and denominator by $n\log(n+1)$, the ratio is
$$\frac{1+\frac1n}{2+\frac1n+\frac{n^2\log(1+1/n)}{n\log(n+1)}}\longrightarrow\frac{1}{2+0}=\frac12 .$$

**Answer:** $\frac12$.

vtrmc-1992-08.title: Count LGG's position by position
vtrmc-1992-08.body:
Count pairs (configuration, position $i$) such that goblin $i$ is an LGG. Fix a position $i$ with $d_i$ neighbours.
- If goblin $i$ is $3'$, it is always an LGG: the other $N-1$ goblins are arbitrary, giving $2^{N-1}$ configurations.
- If goblin $i$ is $2'$, it is an LGG exactly when all its neighbours are $2'$: the remaining $N-1-d_i$ goblins are arbitrary, giving $2^{N-1-d_i}$ configurations.

For $N=1$: $d_1=0$, so $G(1)=1+1=2$. For $N\ge2$ the two end positions have $d_i=1$ and the $N-2$ inner positions have $d_i=2$, so
$$G(N)=N\cdot2^{N-1}+2\cdot2^{N-2}+(N-2)\cdot2^{N-3}=2^{N-3}\bigl(4N+4+N-2\bigr)=(5N+2)\,2^{N-3}.$$
Check: $G(2)=\frac{12}{2}=6$. In particular
$$G(3)=17,\qquad G(4)=22\cdot2=44,$$
which agrees with listing all $8$ resp. $16$ rows (a computer enumeration gives $2,6,17,44,108,256,\dots$ for $N=1,2,3,\dots$).

**Answer:** $G(3)=17$, $G(4)=44$, $G(1)=2$ and $G(N)=(5N+2)2^{N-3}$ for $N\ge2$. ∎

vtrmc-1992-08.title: Recurrence by appending a goblin
vtrmc-1992-08.body:
Let $N\ge2$ and let $X$ be a row of $N$ goblins; every row of $N+1$ goblins is $X2$ or $X3$ (a goblin of height $2'$ or $3'$ appended at the right). Only the new goblin and the old last goblin can change status.
- **Appending $3$.** The new goblin is an LGG. The old last goblin keeps its status if it is a $3$; if it is a $2$, it loses LGG status if it had it, i.e. if $X$ ends in $22$. So $X3$ has one LGG more than $X$ unless $X$ ends in $22$, when it has the same number. There are $2^{N-1}+2^{N-2}$ rows $X$ ending in $3$ or in $32$.
- **Appending $2$.** No old goblin changes status, and the new goblin is an LGG exactly when $X$ ends in $2$. There are $2^{N-1}$ such rows.

Hence, summing over all $2^N$ rows $X$,
$$G(N+1)=2G(N)+2^{N-1}+2^{N-2}+2^{N-1}=2G(N)+5\cdot2^{N-2}.$$
Starting from $G(2)=6$ we get $G(3)=12+5=17$ and $G(4)=34+10=44$. The formula $G(N)=(5N+2)2^{N-3}$ holds for $N=2$, and if it holds for $N$ then
$$2(5N+2)2^{N-3}+5\cdot2^{N-2}=(5N+2+5)2^{N-2}=(5(N+1)+2)2^{(N+1)-3},$$
so it holds for all $N\ge2$ by induction; separately $G(1)=2$. ∎
